questions.question: What is Git and why is it called a distributed version control system?
questions.title: What Is Git?
questions.direct_answer: Git is a distributed version control system where every developer has a complete copy of the project history on their local machine, not just the latest files. This means you can commit changes, create branches, and view history without any network connection, unlike centralized systems that require constant server access.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the core architecture of Git and what 'distributed' means in practical terms beyond just buzzwords
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Git with GitHub or thinking distributed just means multiple people can use it — the key is that everyone has the full history locally
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that distributed means you can work completely offline and that operations like log, diff, and branch are instant because they're local

sections.title: Understanding Git as a Distributed VCS
sections.content:
Git is a **version control system** that tracks changes to files over time, letting teams collaborate on code without overwriting each other's work. The word **distributed** is the key differentiator. In older centralized systems like SVN, there's one master server holding the entire project history, and developers only have working copies of the latest code. If the server goes down, nobody can commit or view history. Git flips this model: when you clone a Git repository, you get the **entire project history** on your local machine — every commit, every branch, every tag.

Think of it like downloading a full backup of Wikipedia instead of just viewing pages through a browser. This architecture means most Git operations (commit, log, diff, branch) are **lightning fast** because they're reading from your local disk, not a remote server. You can work on a plane, commit your changes, create experimental branches, and only push to the server when you're ready and have internet. The distributed nature also provides redundancy — if the central server fails, any developer's copy can restore the full history.

sections.title: Setting Up and Using a Local Git Repository
When Git's Distributed Model Shines
sections.content: Use Git's distributed capabilities when **working remotely or with unreliable internet** — you can commit, branch, and review history during your commute or at a coffee shop with no WiFi. It's essential for **open-source projects** where hundreds of contributors fork the repository and work independently before submitting pull requests. In **enterprise Java projects**, even if you have stable network, the speed of local operations (viewing logs, creating branches, running diffs) makes daily development faster than centralized systems. The distributed model also provides **disaster recovery** — if your company's GitHub or GitLab server crashes, any developer can push their local copy to a new server and restore everything.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing Git with GitHub**: Git is the version control tool that runs on your machine; GitHub is just one hosting service for Git repositories (GitLab and Bitbucket are alternatives). Git existed years before GitHub.
- **Thinking distributed means cloud-based**: Distributed doesn't mean your code is in the cloud — it means every developer has a full copy locally. You can use Git without ever touching the internet.
- **Not understanding offline capability**: Freshers often think they need internet to commit or branch, so they wait to commit until they're online, leading to huge commits instead of small logical ones.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Distributed architecture**: Every clone contains the complete project history, not just current files
**Offline operations**: You can commit, branch, view logs, and diff entirely without network access
**Speed advantage**: Local operations are 10-100x faster than centralized systems querying a remote server
**Redundancy**: If the central server fails, any developer's repository can restore everything
**Git vs GitHub**: Git is the version control tool; GitHub/GitLab are hosting services built around Git
**.git folder**: Contains the entire repository database — deleting this loses all history
**Eventual synchronization**: You work locally and push/pull to sync with teammates when ready

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Git is a distributed version control system, which means when I clone a repository, I'm not just downloading the current code files — I'm getting the entire history of every commit, every branch, and every tag. That full copy sits in the hidden dot-git folder on my machine. The practical benefit is that most operations are completely local and super fast. If I want to see who changed a file six months ago, I run git log and it's instant because it's reading from my local disk, not a remote server. I can commit changes, create branches, and experiment without any network connection. This is really different from older centralized systems like SVN where there's one master server and you need network access for almost everything. In those systems, if the server goes down, you can't commit or view history. With Git, every developer's copy is a full backup. When I'm ready to share my work, I push my commits to a remote repository on GitHub or GitLab, but all the actual Git operations happen locally first. One thing freshers often mix up is thinking Git and GitHub are the same thing — Git is the tool, GitHub is just a hosting service. You can use Git entirely on your own machine without ever touching GitHub. The distributed model also means I can work on a train or at a coffee shop with no WiFi and still make meaningful progress with proper version control. That offline capability is a huge advantage for modern development workflows.

questions.question: How does Git differ from SVN (Subversion)?
questions.title: Git vs SVN
questions.direct_answer: Git is distributed where each developer has the full repository history locally; SVN is centralized where history lives only on a central server. Git allows offline commits and instant branching; SVN requires network access for most operations and branching is slow because it involves server-side copies. Git tracks content snapshots; SVN tracks file revisions incrementally.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of architectural differences between distributed and centralized version control and their practical implications
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Just saying Git is modern and better without explaining concrete differences — always provide specific examples of how workflows differ
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that SVN's simpler permission model is why some large enterprises still use it for code with strict access control requirements

sections.title: Git vs SVN: Architectural Foundations
sections.content:
Git and SVN solve the same problem — letting teams collaborate on code — but with fundamentally different architectures. **SVN (Subversion)** is a **centralized version control system**: there's one authoritative server holding the entire project history, and developers check out working copies of specific revisions.

Think of it like a library where you borrow a book (checkout), make notes, and return it (commit). The library catalog is always on the server. **Git** is **distributed**: every developer clones the entire repository including all history. It's like every developer has their own library with all the books. SVN was the industry standard in the 2000s and is still used in some enterprises. The centralized model makes access control simpler (the server controls who can read/write), but it creates a single point of failure. Git's distributed model provides redundancy and speed but requires different security approaches. For a Java fresher joining a team, you'll almost certainly use Git, but understanding SVN helps you appreciate why Git's design choices matter.

sections.title: Git Is Local, SVN Needs the Server
sections.content:
```bash
# Git: full history is local — these all work with NO network
git log --oneline          # instant, reads local .git
git checkout -b feature     # branch = lightweight pointer, instant
git commit -m "work"        # commits to LOCAL repo, offline is fine
git push origin feature     # only THIS step needs the network

# SVN equivalents need the central server for almost everything:
# svn commit -m "work"                  # fails with no network
# svn copy ^/trunk ^/branches/feature   # server-side copy, slow
```

sections.title: Choosing Between Git and SVN
sections.content:
Use **Git** for modern software projects where developers work remotely, need fast branching for feature development, and want the safety of distributed backups. It's the default choice for web applications, microservices, and open-source projects. Git shines when your team uses pull requests for code review.

Use **SVN** in legacy enterprise environments where strict path-based permissions are required (restricting access to specific folders within a repo), or when your team is already invested in SVN and migration costs outweigh benefits. Some large organizations use SVN for monolithic codebases where fine-grained access control to subsystems is critical. In practice, most Java freshers will only encounter Git, as SVN usage has declined significantly since 2010.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Saying Git is universally better**: While Git dominates today, SVN's simpler permission model genuinely matters in some contexts — blanket statements sound uninformed.
- **Not understanding the offline difference**: Freshers say Git is distributed but can't explain that in SVN you must be online to commit or view history, while Git lets you commit locally and sync later.
- **Thinking SVN branches are like Git branches**: In SVN, a branch is a full server-side copy of the codebase (slow, storage-heavy); in Git, a branch is just a 41-byte pointer to a commit (instant). This architectural difference fundamentally changes how teams use branching.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Centralized vs distributed**: SVN has one source of truth on server; Git has full history in every clone
**Network dependency**: SVN requires server access for commit and log; Git works entirely offline
**Branching cost**: Git branches are instant pointers; SVN branches are expensive server-side directory copies
**Storage model**: Git clones are larger (full history) but operations are faster; SVN working copies are smaller
**Access control**: SVN has built-in path-based permissions; Git relies on hosting layer (GitHub teams, GitLab groups)
**Revision identifiers**: SVN uses sequential numbers (r1234); Git uses SHA-1 hashes (3a7f2e1c...)
**Industry adoption**: Git dominates modern development; SVN remains in some legacy enterprise systems

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The main difference is that Git is distributed and SVN is centralized. In SVN, there's one central server that holds the entire project history. When I check out code, I only get the current files — a working copy. If I want to commit changes or see who modified a file last month, I need to talk to the server. If the server is down or I don't have internet, I'm stuck. Git flips this completely. When I clone a Git repository, I get the entire history on my local machine. I can commit changes, create branches, and review the full project history without any network connection. The commits go into my local repository, and I push them to a remote server when I'm ready. This makes Git way faster for daily operations because everything is reading from my local disk. Another big difference is branching. In SVN, creating a branch means copying the entire project on the server, which is slow and uses a lot of storage. In Git, a branch is just a lightweight pointer to a commit, so creating one is instant and uses almost no space. That's why Git teams create feature branches constantly, while SVN teams traditionally worked on trunk. Now, one thing SVN does better is access control. Because everything goes through the central server, you can set permissions at the folder level — like restricting access to the payments module. Git doesn't have built-in permissions like that; you configure access at the hosting level through GitHub teams or GitLab groups. That's why some large enterprises with strict security requirements still use SVN. But for most modern Java projects, especially if your team does code reviews through pull requests, Git is the standard. It's faster, works offline, and handles branching in a way that supports modern development workflows.

questions.question: What are the three areas (or stages) in Git's local workflow?
questions.title: Git's Three Areas: Working Directory, Staging Area, Repository
questions.direct_answer: Git has three areas: the working directory where you edit files, the staging area (also called the index) where you prepare changes for the next commit, and the local repository where committed snapshots are permanently stored in the dot-git folder. This three-stage model lets you craft precise commits by staging only specific changes instead of committing everything at once.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Git's internal workflow model, which is fundamental to using commands like git add, git commit, git reset, and git stash correctly
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking git commit goes directly from working directory to repository, skipping the staging area — this misunderstanding causes confusion with commands like git add
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the staging area enables atomic logical commits by letting you commit only part of your changes, even from within a single file using git add -p

sections.title: Git's Three-Stage Architecture
sections.content:
Git organizes your work into three distinct areas, and understanding these is essential for using Git effectively. The **working directory** is simply the files and folders you see in your project — this is where you edit code in your IDE. When you save changes to a Java file, those changes exist only in the working directory. The **staging area** (also called the **index**) is a holding zone for changes you want to include in the next commit.

Think of it as a shopping cart: you select specific items (file changes) to purchase (commit) rather than buying everything in the store. You move changes from working directory to staging area with the git add command. The **local repository** is the permanent storage in the hidden dot-git folder where Git saves committed snapshots. Once you run git commit, the staged changes become a permanent part of project history. This three-stage model is unique to Git — tools like SVN commit directly from working directory to server. The staging area might seem like extra complexity at first, but it gives you powerful control: you can stage only some files, or even specific lines within a file, enabling clean logical commits instead of messy everything commits.

sections.title: The Three Areas at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Working directory|~Files you edit|your project files in the IDE|changes start here|git status shows them as unstaged
amber|Staging area (index)|~The next commit, previewed|git add moves changes here|stage part of your work|enables clean, logical commits
emerald|Local repository|~The .git folder|git commit saves a snapshot|permanent project history|lives entirely offline
rose|The flow|~edit -> add -> commit|working -> staging -> repo|commits never skip staging|run git status to stay oriented

sections.title: Working with Git's Three Stages
When the Three-Stage Model Matters
sections.content:
The staging area becomes critical when **you've made multiple unrelated changes** and need to commit them as separate logical units. For example, you fixed a bug in OrderService and refactored formatting in three other files. Stage and commit the bug fix first, then stage and commit the refactoring — this keeps history clean.

Use the staging area for **partial commits during feature development**: you've added both the happy path and error handling, but error handling isn't done yet. Stage only the happy path files, commit them, and continue working on error handling. The staging area also enables **interactive staging** with git add -p (patch mode), where you can select specific code chunks within a file to stage, leaving other chunks unstaged. This is powerful when a single file has both completed and in-progress work.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using git commit -a blindly**: The dash-a flag stages all tracked files automatically, bypassing the staging area. Freshers use this to avoid typing git add, but it defeats the purpose of the three-stage model and leads to messy commits with unrelated changes.
- **Not understanding git reset**: Freshers think reset deletes changes, but git reset HEAD file just unstages a file, moving it from staging area back to working directory — the changes are still there.
- **Confusing staged with committed**: After git add, changes are staged but not saved permanently. You must still run git commit. If you switch branches without committing, staged changes come with you to the new branch.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Working directory**: The visible project files where you edit code in your IDE
**Staging area (index)**: A preparation zone holding changes selected for the next commit via git add
**Local repository**: Permanent storage in dot-git folder where committed snapshots live
**git add command**: Moves changes from working directory to staging area — does not commit anything
**git commit command**: Takes everything in staging area and saves it permanently as a snapshot
**Logical commits**: The staging area lets you commit only related changes, keeping history meaningful
**git status**: Shows what's in working directory vs staging area — run this constantly to stay oriented

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Git has three areas that changes flow through. First is the working directory, which is just the regular files and folders I see in my project. When I edit a Java file in IntelliJ and save it, that change exists in the working directory. Second is the staging area, which people also call the index. This is like a preparation zone for the next commit. When I run git add on a file, I'm copying that change from the working directory into the staging area. It's not committed yet, it's just marked as ready to commit. The third area is the local repository, which is the permanent storage inside the hidden dot-git folder. When I run git commit, everything in the staging area gets saved as a snapshot in the repository. The key insight is that commits don't go directly from working directory to repository — they must pass through staging first. This might seem like extra work, but it gives you precise control. Let's say I've fixed a bug in OrderService and also refactored some formatting in three other files. I want those to be separate commits because they're unrelated changes. I can run git add OrderService.java to stage just the bug fix, commit it, then stage and commit the refactoring files separately. Without the staging area, I'd have to commit everything at once, which makes history messy. A common mistake freshers make is using git commit dash-a, which auto-stages all changes. That bypasses the whole point of the staging area and leads to kitchen-sink commits with unrelated stuff mixed together. Another mistake is thinking git add saves changes permanently — it doesn't. Add just stages them. You still need to commit. If you're ever confused about what's where, run git status. It clearly shows which files are in working directory only, which are staged, and which are committed.

questions.question: What is the difference between git init and git clone?
questions.title: git init vs git clone
questions.direct_answer: git init creates a brand new empty Git repository in the current directory by setting up the dot-git folder structure. git clone copies an existing remote repository (including all commits, branches, and tags) to your local machine and automatically configures the origin remote. Use init for starting a new project from scratch; use clone when joining an existing project.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic command knowledge and understanding when to use each — tests whether the candidate knows the typical workflows for starting vs joining projects
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using git init on a folder and then manually adding a remote when they should have just used git clone to pull down an existing GitHub repo
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that git clone automatically sets up remote tracking branches and configures your local main or master branch to track origin main

sections.title: git init vs git clone: Starting Points
sections.content:
Both commands create a Git repository, but they're used in completely different scenarios. **git init** initializes a brand new Git repository from scratch in your current directory. It creates the hidden dot-git folder with the necessary database structure, but the repository is empty — no commits, no branches yet. You use init when you're starting a new Java project on your laptop and want to add version control. After running init, you typically add files, make your first commit, and optionally connect to a remote repository later with git remote add. **git clone** copies an existing repository from a remote location (like GitHub, GitLab, or another developer's machine) to your local system. When you clone, you get the entire project history — every commit, every branch, every tag. Git also automatically sets up a **remote** called origin pointing back to the source repository, and configures your local main branch to track the remote main branch. You use clone when joining an existing team project, contributing to open-source, or setting up the codebase on a new laptop.

For freshers, clone is by far the more common command because you're usually joining existing projects, not creating them.

sections.title: init vs clone in Commands
sections.content:
```bash
# git init — brand new empty repo; you wire up the remote yourself
git init                                   # creates .git, no commits yet
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git remote add origin https://github.com/me/new-project.git
git push -u origin main

# git clone — copy an existing repo; origin + tracking set up for you
git clone https://github.com/company/order-service.git
cd order-service
git remote -v        # origin is already configured
git pull             # works immediately, no setup needed
```

emerald|git clone|~Join an existing repo|downloads full history|sets up origin + tracking|the common fresher case
amber|After init|~You wire it up|make the first commit|git remote add origin|then git push -u
rose|After clone|~Ready to work|origin already set|local main tracks origin/main|just pull and push

sections.title: Choosing Between init and clone
sections.content:
Use **git init** when you're creating a brand new Java project from scratch — maybe a personal learning project or a new microservice. Run it in your project folder after setting up the initial file structure. After the first commit, you can optionally push to GitHub by creating a repo there and running git remote add origin <url> followed by git push.

Use **git clone** when the repository already exists somewhere else. This is the typical scenario for freshers: your team lead sends you a GitHub URL, you run git clone https://github.com/company/order-service.git, and you get the entire codebase with history. Clone also works for setting up the same project on multiple machines — clone it on your work laptop, then clone again on your home desktop. One subtle point: if your company uses a repository template, you might clone that template and then remove the origin remote to start fresh.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using init when you should clone**: Freshers see a GitHub repo URL, run git init locally, copy files manually, and try to push — this creates a disconnected repo. Just git clone the URL instead.
- **Not understanding origin**: After git clone, freshers don't realize that origin is just a nickname for the remote URL. They think origin is a special Git keyword. It's just a conventional name that clone sets up for you.
- **Re-cloning unnecessarily**: If you accidentally delete your working directory files but the dot-git folder is intact, you don't need to re-clone. Just run git checkout to restore files. Cloning creates a new repository, which you don't need if you already have the Git history locally.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **git init**: Creates a new empty repository in the current directory — used for starting projects from scratch
**git clone <url>**: Copies an existing remote repository with full history — used for joining existing projects
**Remote configuration**: clone automatically sets up origin remote; init does not configure any remotes
**Tracking branches**: clone configures your local main to track origin/main; init doesn't have branches until first commit
**Common workflow**: Freshers typically clone existing repos, not init new ones — you're joining teams, not starting companies
**URL formats**: clone accepts HTTPS (https://github.com/user/repo.git) or SSH (git@github.com:user/repo.git)
**Target directory**: git clone <url> creates a subfolder named after the repo; git clone <url> <name> uses custom name

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: git init and git clone both create a Git repository, but they're used in completely different situations. I'd use git init when I'm starting a brand new project from scratch on my local machine. Let's say I create a new Java project in IntelliJ for a personal learning exercise. I'd navigate to that project folder in the terminal and run git init. This creates the hidden dot-git folder, which is where Git stores all the repository data. At that point, the repository is empty — no commits yet, no branches. I'd then add my initial files and make my first commit. If I later want to push this to GitHub, I'd create a repo there, then run git remote add origin with the GitHub URL, and finally git push. On the other hand, git clone is what I'd use when I'm joining an existing project. This is way more common for freshers. My manager sends me a GitHub link to the team's order service repository. I run git clone followed by that URL, and Git downloads the entire repository to my machine — every commit, every branch, the full history. The clone command also does something smart: it automatically sets up a remote called origin that points back to the GitHub repo, and it configures my local main branch to track the remote main branch. That means I can just run git pull and git push without extra setup. One mistake I've seen is when people run git init for a project that already exists on GitHub. They think they need to init first and then connect it, but that's backwards. If the repo already exists remotely, just clone it. You only init when you're creating something brand new. Another thing to know is that git clone creates a subdirectory named after the repository. If I clone order-service, I'll get an order-service folder. I can customize that by adding a directory name at the end of the clone command. So to summarize: init is for starting a new project from zero, clone is for copying an existing repo. For most freshers, clone is what you'll use ninety percent of the time because you're joining teams and working on existing codebases.

questions.question: Is a Git commit a diff (set of changes) or a snapshot of the entire project?
questions.title: Git Commits Are Snapshots, Not Diffs
questions.direct_answer: A Git commit is a snapshot of all tracked files at that moment, not a diff. Each commit stores a complete tree structure pointing to file contents, so Git knows the exact state of every file. Git internally optimizes storage by only saving changed content using content-addressable storage, but conceptually every commit is a full snapshot of the project.

interviewer_intent.testing: Deep understanding of Git's data model — this separates candidates who've studied Git internals from those who only know surface commands
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying commits store only the changed lines like SVN does — this is backwards from how Git actually works and leads to misunderstanding commands like git checkout
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Git uses SHA-1 hashing and blob objects to store file contents, with trees linking blobs, and that Git packs files efficiently despite the snapshot model

sections.title: Git Commits as Snapshots, Not Diffs
sections.content:
This is one of Git's most misunderstood concepts. A **commit is a complete snapshot** of all tracked files at that point in time, not a delta or diff from the previous commit. When you commit, Git doesn't record that you changed line 42 in OrderService.java from X to Y. Instead, it captures the entire state of every tracked file. Each commit contains a **tree object** that lists every file and its content at that moment.

Think of it like taking a photo of your project — the photo shows everything, not just what changed since the last photo. This is fundamentally different from tools like SVN, which store commits as changesets (diffs applied to previous versions). Why does Git do this? Because snapshots make certain operations incredibly fast. When you run git checkout to switch to an old commit, Git just restores that snapshot directly — it doesn't have to replay hundreds of diffs. When you compare two commits, Git has both full states and can compute the diff on demand. Now, Git isn't wasteful — it uses **content-addressable storage** with SHA-1 hashes. If a file doesn't change between commits, Git doesn't duplicate it; both commits point to the same stored content. Git also periodically packs objects to save space. But conceptually, every commit is a full snapshot.

sections.title: Visualizing Snapshots in Git History
Why Snapshots Matter in Practice
sections.content: Understanding snapshots helps when **checking out old code** — you're restoring a complete project state, not undoing changes one by one. This makes time travel fast and reliable. It's crucial for **branching decisions**: because commits are snapshots, creating a branch is just making a pointer to a commit, not copying files. The snapshot model also explains **why Git is fast at merging** — it compares three complete snapshots (your branch, target branch, and common ancestor) to determine conflicts, rather than replaying diffs. For **debugging with git bisect**, Git can jump directly to any commit snapshot to test if a bug exists, without reconstructing state from hundreds of deltas. Knowing this helps you **trust Git's integrity** — because commits are snapshots with SHA-1 hashes, any corruption is immediately detected.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking commits store diffs**: This is how SVN works, not Git. In Git, diffs are computed on demand by comparing snapshots. Saying commits store diffs in an interview immediately reveals shallow Git knowledge.
- **Worrying about repository size**: Freshers think the snapshot model wastes space, but Git's content-addressable storage means unchanged files aren't duplicated. Git periodically packs objects efficiently.
- **Not understanding checkout behavior**: Because commits are snapshots, git checkout replaces your working directory with that snapshot — it's not replaying or undoing changes, it's swapping the entire state. This can be disorienting if you expect diff-based behavior.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Snapshot model**: Each commit stores the complete state of all tracked files, not a diff from the previous commit
**Tree objects**: Commits contain trees that list every file and point to blob objects holding file contents
**Content-addressable storage**: Git uses SHA-1 hashing; unchanged files aren't duplicated across commits
**Fast operations**: Snapshots enable instant checkout, efficient merging, and fast bisect — no diff replay needed
**Git vs SVN**: SVN stores commits as changesets (deltas); Git stores commits as snapshots
**Space efficiency**: Git packs objects periodically, compressing similar content to save space despite snapshot model
**Integrity**: Each commit's SHA-1 hash depends on its entire tree, making corruption immediately detectable

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A Git commit is a snapshot of the entire project, not a diff. This trips up a lot of people because tools like SVN store commits as changesets — records of what lines changed. Git doesn't work that way. When I make a commit, Git captures the complete state of every tracked file at that moment. Each commit has a tree object that lists all the files and directories, and each file points to a blob object storing that file's content. It's like taking a photograph of the project. The photo shows everything, not just what's different from the last photo. Now, you might think this wastes a ton of space, but Git is smarter than that. It uses content-addressable storage with SHA-1 hashes. If I commit and OrderService.java hasn't changed since the last commit, Git doesn't duplicate that file — both commits point to the same blob object. Git also runs garbage collection periodically, packing objects and compressing similar files to save space. But conceptually, every commit is a full snapshot. The reason Git does this is speed. When I run git checkout to go back to an old commit, Git just restores that snapshot directly. It doesn't have to replay a hundred diffs to reconstruct the old state. When I compare two commits with git diff, Git has both complete snapshots and computes the differences on the fly. This also makes branching super cheap — a branch is just a pointer to a commit snapshot, not a copy of files. A common mistake freshers make is saying commits store diffs because that's more intuitive from other version control systems. But in Git, diffs are derived by comparing snapshots, not stored directly. Understanding this helps you reason about commands like checkout and merge — they're manipulating snapshots, not replaying changes. It also explains why Git can detect file corruption so reliably — every commit's hash depends on the complete tree of file contents, so any bit flip breaks the hash chain immediately.
